newsitem.title: USA: U.S. readies flu vaccine mix for next winter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. readies flu vaccine mix for next winter.

text.p: Federal health officials said Thursday the vaccine for the 1997-98 flu season will be altered to reflect a recent change in one of the three influenza strains circulating worldwide.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the recommended vaccine for next winter's flu season reflected the emergence in other countries of a new type A(H1N1) flu strain. It is not uncommon for type A flu strains to mutate or change from year to year.

The recommended 1997-98 flu vaccine will protect against the new virus, which was not seen in the United States during the flu season that just ended. The recommended vaccine will also offer protection against type A(H3N2) and type B viruses.

"Of the three components, one of them will change and that is the type A(H1N1) virus which has actually circulated at very low levels in most parts of the world this past season," CDC epidemiologist Nancy Arden said.
Of laboratory specimens tested during the winter, 81 percent were influenza type A and 19 percent were type B. In February and March, 88 percent of specimens tested were influenza type B.
"We have not seen high levels of influenza B in several years now, so we would expect to see more influenza B next year," Arden said.
Last winter's flu season peaked in January. During the week ending April 5, only Alaska and Arizona were reporting flu outbreaks, the CDC said.

"It was a more severe season than average, probably because it was a predominantly type A(H3N2) season and that is associated with illness in all age groups and mortality, especially in the elderly," Arden said.
Because of the time required to manufacture flu vaccine, researchers must predict every spring which influenza viruses they expect to circulate during the following winter.
The CDC estimates that about 20,000 Americans die from influenza or its complications every year.
